segments: Declarative Docker configuration on NixOS. Docker and Podman use different approaches and different NixOS configuration interfaces; check them against the relevant version.
NixOS has a built-in module for declaring containers directly, similar to a simplified Compose:

Limitations: this module does not implement the full Compose model. Its own dependsOn generates systemd After/Requires dependencies, and health/runtime options can be supplied through the corresponding interfaces or extraOptions, but it does not automatically provide Compose profiles or service_healthy dependency semantics. For complex applications, using docker compose and keeping the Compose file in Git remains the recommended approach.

Docker is primarily managed through system-level configuration. Do not configure credentials by writing a config.json containing auth/token data into the store as public home.file text. Separately verify support in the relevant system or user modules for a user-level rootless daemon, socket, and context.
Choosing Docker vs. Podman on NixOS
The engines can coexist, but CLI and socket compatibility options may conflict. When enabling actual Docker, do not also let Podman take over the docker command:
Verifying Builds, Activation, and Runtime Behavior

nixos-rebuild build only verifies build outputs. The example switch activates the system and may restart services, so follow the deployment procedure. Logging in again after joining the docker group only determines when the permission change takes effect; it does not reduce the group's security risk. The controlled file /run/secrets/postgres.env must exist with restricted read access and contain the required database credentials; this configuration does not generate it automatically. Rootless mode uses a separate daemon/socket; running the CLI as an ordinary user does not automatically make the setup rootless.
